hints: Look for carbon atoms joined to four different atoms or groups, focus on the two alpha carbons next to C=O groups in the centre of Fig. 8.1.
walkthrough:
Apply the chirality test**
Picture yourself sitting with the structure. A carbon is chiral only if it has four completely different groups attached. Ignore $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$ and $\text{C=O}$ carbons straight away because they either have repeated H or methyl groups or only three groups.

Spot the two alpha carbons**
There are two carbons that each carry H, N and two different carbon chains. One is the aspartic acid alpha carbon, $\text{NH-CH(CH}_2\text{COOH)-C=O}$, and the other is the phenylalanine alpha carbon, $\text{NH-CH(CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-COOCH}_3$. Each has four different substituents, so there are 2 chiral centres.

hints: Scan Fig. 8.1 from left to right and label each N and each C=O separately, remembering the arene is already given so do not count it again.
walkthrough:
Find the nitrogen groups**
Look at the two nitrogens. On the left, $-\text{NH}-$ is joined to two carbons only, with no C=O directly attached to N. That is a secondary amine. In the middle, $-\text{C(=O)-NH}-$ is a carbonyl directly joined to nitrogen. That is the classic amide, here a peptide link.

Find the oxygen groups**
Now look at the three C=O groups. At the bottom left, $-\text{C(=O)OH}$ is a carboxylic acid. On the right, $-\text{C(=O)OCH}_3$ is a carbonyl joined to O joined to carbon, so an ester. Together with the arene already named, the other groups are amide, amine, ester and carboxylic acid.
Final answer: amide, amine (secondary amine), ester, carboxylic acid / carboxyl

hints: Think what hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ does to a $\text{C(=O)-N}$ link and to a $\text{C(=O)-O-C}$ link.
Think what $\text{NaOH}$ does to a $-\text{COOH}$ group even in the cold, with no bond to carbon breaking.
walkthrough:
Separate bond breaking from proton transfer**
Hot $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ can do two quite different jobs. It can attack a carbonyl carbon and split the molecule in two, and it can simply remove an acidic proton with no carbon skeleton breaking.

Assign each job to neotame**
The central amide $\text{C(=O)-NH}$ and the terminal ester $\text{C(=O)OCH}_3$ are both split by $\text{OH}^-$ to give carboxylate salts plus amine and alcohol. That is hydrolysis. The free $-\text{COOH}$ group simply loses $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$ to give $-\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ plus water. That is acid-base, also called neutralisation.

Final answer: 1 hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis of amide and ester)
2 acid-base / neutralisation (of carboxylic acid to carboxylate)

hints: Mark the two cleavage points, the amide $\text{C(=O)-NH}$ in the middle and the ester $\text{C(=O)-OCH}_3$ on the right, the left amine link stays intact.
Recall that in excess hot $\text{NaOH}$ every $-\text{COOH}$ and every new $-\text{COOH}$ formed by hydrolysis exists as $-\text{COONa}$.
Count fragments, cleavage of one amide plus one ester plus neutralisation gives a large dicarboxylate fragment, a smaller amino carboxylate fragment and a small alcohol.
walkthrough:
Cut the central amide**
Focus on $\text{...CH-C(=O)-NH-CH...}$ in the middle. Alkaline hydrolysis adds water across that bond. The carbonyl side becomes a carboxylate, $\text{...CH-COO}^-$, and the nitrogen side becomes a free amine, $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH...}$. So neotame splits into a left aspartame-like piece and a right phenylalanine-like piece.

Build the left product**
The left piece keeps the $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}-$ group attached to the aspartic acid alpha carbon. It now has two carboxyl groups, the original side chain $-\text{COOH}$ and the new one from amide hydrolysis. In excess $\text{NaOH}$ both are $\text{COONa}$. That gives $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH(COONa)CH}_2\text{COONa}$.

Build the right product and methanol**
The right piece is $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH(CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-COOCH}_3$ immediately after amide cleavage. The methyl ester then hydrolyses: $\text{COOCH}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{COO}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. In excess alkali the acid is $\text{COONa}$, so you get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)COONa}$ plus $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. Those three structures are the three organic products.
